TAMARIND
Family  Leguminosae
Scientific name Tamarindus indica
Common name tamarind, Indian date
a flavoring in East Indian and Middle
Eastern dishes, in much the same way
lemon juice is used in Western cuisine.
Tamarind’s sweet-sour flavor combines
well with the spicy flavor of chili in the
Thai and Vietnamese cuisines, where
unripe pods are used in soups and stews.
In Indian cooking, tamarind is used as a
seasoning in lentil and bean dishes and in
the dish called “vindaloo.”  Tamarind
syrup, which can be found in Dutch,
Indonesian, and East Indian markets, is
used to flavor soft drinks.
Nutrient composition
In the amounts customarily eaten,
tamarind is not a significant source of
nutrients.
Mexico and Central and South America.
Belize, Brazil, Guatemala, and India are
the major commercial producers of
tamarind worldwide.  The tree is a slow-
growing, long-lived evergreen with supple
branches and bright-green leaves that
appear in pairs, 1 to 2-1/2 inches in
length, and fold up at night.  Under favor-
able conditions, the tree may grow up to
80 feet tall and 20 to 35 feet wide.  In
severe drought, the leaves often drop off
the tree.  A young tree bears fruit within
4 years and continues to fruit for up to
60 years.  Tamarind fruits may be left on
the tree for up to 6 months after maturity
without loss of moisture.
Uses
Tamarind is available in Indian and Asian
markets as a fresh fruit, as a concentrated
pulp with seeds, as a paste, as whole pods
